# True or false: Business owners

For owners and managers of clinics, schools, shops and other businesses that use software but do not build it. No technical knowledge needed.

10 statements (Foundation 6, Standard 4). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area business-owners`.

### 1. Multi-factor sign-in on the email account should come before any other account.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Email can reset the password of almost every other service, so whoever controls it controls the rest. Turn on multi-factor authentication for email first, then banking, accounting and admin accounts. Prefer an app or a security key to text-message codes.

Read more: [leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md](../../leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md)

</details>

### 2. A backup disk that stays plugged into the office computer protects the business against ransomware.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Ransomware encrypts every drive it can reach, including a backup disk that is always connected. Keep at least one copy offline, or on storage that cannot be changed or deleted for a set period. Then test a restore every 3 months.

Read more: [leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md](../../leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md)

</details>

### 3. Until you have restored from a backup, you do not know how long the business would be stopped.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** A backup can be incomplete, and a restore can take days instead of hours. Ask your IT provider to restore a folder and one key system every 3 months and write down the time. Compare it with how long the business can cope without that system.

Read more: [leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md](../../leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md)

</details>

### 4. It is fine for the IT provider to own the business's domain name and admin accounts if the provider is trusted.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** If the provider owns them, a dispute, a failure or a breach at the provider can lock you out of your own email and website. Put the domain, admin accounts and backups in the business's name. Keep a copy of the admin credentials that the owner controls.

Read more: [leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md](../../leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md)

</details>

### 5. In the first hour of a ransomware attack, wiping and reinstalling the affected computers destroys evidence that the insurer and responders need.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Disconnect affected computers from the network but do not switch them off, wipe or reinstall them. Responders use what is on them to find out how the attacker got in and what was taken. Call your insurer early: many policies require notice before you act.

Read more: [leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md](../../leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md)

</details>

### 6. Staff may paste patient or customer records into a free AI chat tool if they delete the conversation afterwards.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Deleting the conversation on your screen does not remove it from the service, and free tools may keep or reuse what you type. Approve a few tools with a business account and say which data must never go into them. The staff AI use policy template covers this on one page.

Read more: [leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md](../../leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md)

</details>

### 7. A leaver's access should be removed on their last working day, including shared passwords they knew.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Former staff with working accounts are an easy way in, by mistake or on purpose. Remove access on the last working day and change any shared password the person knew. A password manager makes that change quick.

Read more: [leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md](../../leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md)

</details>

### 8. A business that buys all its software as online subscriptions has no data protection duties, because the supplier holds the data.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** The business usually stays the controller of its customers' and staff data, even when a supplier stores it. You still need to know what data you hold and why, tell people in a privacy notice, and report breaches on time. Check that the supplier's contract covers breach notice, data location and exit.

Read more: [leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md](../../leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md)

</details>

### 9. Before signing up for an online service, a business should check that it can export all its data in a common format.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** If you cannot get your data out, leaving the service later is slow and expensive, and the supplier knows it. Check for export to common formats such as CSV or PDF before you sign. Once a year, export the data from your most important service and open it elsewhere.

Read more: [leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md](../../leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md)

</details>

### 10. Text-message codes are the strongest form of multi-factor sign-in a small business can choose.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Text-message codes are much better than a password alone, but attackers can intercept them or trick staff into reading them out. Authenticator apps are stronger, and security keys or passkeys resist phishing. Use the strongest option each service supports.

Read more: [leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md](../../leaders/for-small-and-medium-businesses.md)

</details>
